chapter_theme: Waking in Champapati's shrine after the prince's killing, Manimekalai casts off her borrowed form and mourns him; the deity of the pillar image, Thuvathikan, forbids her grief, traces the prince's violent deaths to a cook he killed in anger in a former birth, and foretells her imprisonment and release, her voyage, the schools of Vanji, the famine of Kanchi, her teaching by Aravanar, and her release births later as the Buddha's chief disciple.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, a Buddhist renunciant, here waking from the form of Kayachandigai she had taken
the Chola king's son, killed by Kanchanan's sword; Rahulan in a former birth
a deity of the divine host who dwells in the image Mayan carved on the old pillar of the public hall
Attipathi's son, Lakshmi's husband in the former birth (Udayakumaran in this one)
the Buddhist ascetic who foretold the fall of Idavayam and Lakshmi's future births
the cook who carried the meal prepared for Brahmadharman
the divine builder who carved the pillar image
the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father
the aged Buddhist teacher of Puhar (Aravana Adigal)
first holder of the bowl, reborn as the Javaka king
the guardian goddess of the Buddha's seat on Manipallavam
the materialist (Lokayata) debater of Vanji, foretold here
the sea goddess who carried Manimekalai to Manipallavam

manimekalai:21:1-22.reading: Waking in Champapati's shrine beside the pillar carved with a god, Manimekalai learns what the vidyadhara did, what befell the prince and what the pillar image told the killer; crying 'perish this form', she casts off her borrowed shape and laments to the dead prince that she burned herself on his pyre in the birth when he died of the snake's poison glance, that the goddess carried her to Manipallavam where she learned her own and all his births, and that she took Kayachandigai's form only to teach him birth and death and the fruits of dharma and wrong and so end his evil karma.
manimekalai:21:1-22.nuance: Her disguise is given a purpose here that the earlier kaathais did not state: it was a teaching form, meant to save him, and it became the cause of his death, since Kanchanan struck him for approaching 'Kayachandigai'. The pillar image's words to Kanchanan (kaathai 20, lines 110 to 126) are what she 'hears' at lines 5 to 8; the text does not say how a woman lying dazed heard them.
manimekalai:21:1-22.event: Manimekalai wakes in Champapati's shrine, learns of the prince's killing, throws off Kayachandigai's form and laments over him.

claims.claim: those who are born die and the dead are born again, and dharma brings worth as wrong brings suffering

manimekalai:21:23-34.reading: Manimekalai asks whether he died by the deluded wrath of the vidyadhara's sword as his cruel karma ripened, weeps and rises to go to him; the pillar deity stops her, saying that he has been her son and she his daughter, in birth after birth, that the birth she has seen is not the only one, and that one striving to leave the low round of wandering births should not grieve.
manimekalai:21:23-34.nuance: The deity's argument against grief is not that the dead are well but that kinship itself is unstable across births: the husband of one life was a son in another, so the bond she mourns is one turn among many. The unit's speaker changes at 27; the deity is named only at 35.
manimekalai:21:23-34.event: Manimekalai weeps and rises to go to the prince's body, and the pillar deity forbids her to go.

claims.claim: the dead man's death was his own cruel karma coming to ripeness
two beings meet in many births in changing relations, so the present relation is no ground for grief

manimekalai:21:35-44.reading: Manimekalai turns to the voice, asks whether it is the deity of unfailing tongue who dwells in this hall, worships its feet, and asks whether it knows why the prince died by the snake's poison glance in the birth left behind and now by the vidyadhara's sword, begging its grace to be told.
manimekalai:21:35-44.nuance: Her question pairs two deaths across two births and asks for one cause; the deity's answer will give the second death a cause in the first life, not the snake.
manimekalai:21:35-44.event: Manimekalai worships the pillar deity and asks it why the prince died twice by violence.

manimekalai:21:45-60.reading: The deity answers that in the former birth, on the bank of the Kayangarai, she and Rahulan served the sage Brahmadharman and offered to cook him a special meal at dawn; when the cook, coming at daybreak, slipped and fell and broke the vessels, Rahulan, angry that the meal for the ascetic had failed of its hour, cut him through with the sword so that shoulder and head came apart: that was the cruel deed.
manimekalai:21:45-60.nuance: The murder is set inside an act of piety: the anger rises because the gift to the sage is spoiled. The cook's fall is an accident (நடைத் திறத்து இழுக்கி), so the whole weight of the deed lies on the anger.
manimekalai:21:45-60.event: The deity tells how Rahulan, in his former birth, killed with his sword a cook who stumbled and spoilt the meal prepared for Brahmadharman.

manimekalai:21:61-72.reading: The deity draws the lesson: those who say a grievous deed done for one's master is shielded by that master do not know; though done from love of doing dharma, if it is violence its strong karma does not leave, and when it draws near it returns on the life in a later birth; it is that deed which came here and did this harm to her husband.
manimekalai:21:61-72.nuance: The deity names and rejects a defence, that the one served answers for a deed done in his service; intention to serve dharma does not change a killing's fruit. Lines 61 to 62 and 67 to 69 are compressed and the exact construction is unclear, though the sense of 66 and 70 to 71 is plain. Kaathai 20 has the same deity tell the killer Kanchanan that his deed too will not leave him (20:120-129): the prince's karma ripens through a new wrong that is itself accountable.

claims.claim: a cruel deed done for the sake of the one served is not shielded by him
a violent deed keeps its strong karma even when done out of love of dharma
the karma of a deed returns on its doer in a later birth

manimekalai:21:73-86.reading: The deity foretells her near future: the king, grieving his son and hearing the ascetics' true report, will imprison her; the queen, set on keeping her near, will take her from the prison; Madhavi, bowing at the great sage's feet and telling him the trouble, will come with him, and on his word the queen will free her; she will go to Aputtiran, now ruling a kingdom, agree with him in true teaching and sail with him to the island of Manipallavam.
manimekalai:21:73-86.nuance: The queen's motive is given in one word, கொட்பினள், which can mean scheming or set on a purpose; the following kaathais show her tormenting Manimekalai before she relents, which the prophecy passes over.
manimekalai:21:73-86.event: The deity foretells Manimekalai's imprisonment, her release by the queen at the sage's word, and her voyage with Aputtiran.

manimekalai:21:87-111.reading: The deity goes on: after the Javaka king learns his own story from Deepatilakai and returns home, she will leave the island in an ascetic's form and enter Vanji, where learned men will set out the schools' false words: that God our lord made all lives in order, that the formless one who makes other forms is God, that painful austerity cuts this bondage and seats one at the top of the world of bliss, that all is a combining of the elements; and when one declares there is no God, the dead are not reborn and dharma is pointless, she who knows birth and dharma will laugh at him, tell him her former birth, and hear him say a deity deluded her and she was deceived by a dream.
manimekalai:21:87-111.nuance: The four views at 94 to 100 are not named by school; the creator god may be the Brahma-vadin's and the formless maker the Saiva's of kaathai 27, the austerity that seats the soul at the top of the world reads as Jain, and the combining of elements is the materialist's. The prophecy calls them all படிற்று உரை, false talk, but answers only the materialist. Even his rejoinder is foretold: the epic anticipates the objection that knowledge of past births is a dream sent by a god, and the deity's own role in carrying her off makes it pointed. The two materialist claims are marked refuted because the work answers them: here Manimekalai's laugh and her account of her birth (106 to 108), and in kaathai 27 her argument that he knows even his own parents only by inference (27:284-289). The speakers of 107 to 110 are not marked and are read from the sense.
manimekalai:21:87-111.event: The deity foretells Manimekalai's going to Vanji in an ascetic's form, hearing the schools, and mocking the materialist.

claims.claim: God our lord created all living beings in due order
the one who has no form of his own and makes the other forms is God
painful austerity cuts the bond of deeds and seats the soul at the summit of the world of bliss
all things are combinations of the transformed elements
there is no God, the dead are not born again, and dharma serves nothing
knowledge of a former birth is a dream-delusion sent by a deity

manimekalai:21:112-129.reading: The deity tells her not to falter before the materialist but to affirm that evil deeds reach their doer and the dead are reborn; then it explains its own speech: wood, earth, stone and painted images do not speak, but the wise, planning the protection of a guarded city, have craftsmen shape the deities they intend in clay, stone, wood and wall at its streets, temples, old trees, ghats and halls, and those deities never leave their places and tell men of fleshly eyes what will befall.
manimekalai:21:112-129.nuance: The deity concedes the sceptic's premise, that an image as material does not speak, and relocates the voice in a deity bound to the place by the city's founders; the image is a seat, not the speaker. The two halves of the unit go together: the materialist will call her knowledge a god's trick, and the deity's account of how gods speak through images is the apparatus he will deny.

claims.claim: evil deeds reach their doer and the dead are born again
wood, earth, stone and painted images do not themselves speak
deities installed by the wise in images at a city's places stay there and tell mortals what will befall

manimekalai:21:130-146.reading: The deity names itself Thuvathikan, one of the great divine host, who never leaves the image Mayan carved in its likeness on the ancient pillar; it speaks of its close companion Oviyachenan, whom the city paints beside it wherever the two went to play, honouring it with flowers and incense, and bids Manimekalai trust its word; she says she does not doubt and asks for its divine words to the end, and it promises to tell what is to come.
manimekalai:21:130-146.nuance: Line 134, 'what men know the gods do not know', and line 136, 'who told this city what he is?', are hard to place in the argument; they may mean that the townspeople's worship knows the deity better than it knows itself, but that is a guess. The closing quotation mark at 145 sits oddly, so whether 145 to 146 are narrator or deity is unclear.
manimekalai:21:130-146.event: The pillar deity tells its name and its bond to the image, and Manimekalai asks it to tell her future to the end.

manimekalai:21:147-171.reading: Thuvathikan foretells that when rain is withheld and Kanchi of the golden walls loses its beauty as lives perish, she will take the divine vessel kept in this shrine as medicine for lives, go with her mothers to Kanchi where Aravanar also is, cast off her borrowed form there by his grace, and bearing the bowl of dharma that gives rain's plenty to a parched world protect its people; when she tells Aravanar the doctrines of the other schools, he will teach her austerity, dharma, dependent arising and the path that ends becoming, and vow that, dying and being born, he will guard the true doctrine and not leave that place until the Buddha-sun rises.
manimekalai:21:147-171.nuance: The bowl is set against drought itself: அறன் ஓடு, 'the bowl of dharma', gives the plenty that rain would give (157 to 158). Aravanar's vow to keep dying and being born until the next Buddha appears is a vow to stay in the round of births for the teaching's sake, which the same kaathai otherwise urges Manimekalai to escape.
manimekalai:21:147-171.event: Thuvathikan foretells Manimekalai's journey to famine-struck Kanchi with the bowl, and Aravanar's teaching and vow there.

claims.claim: Aravanar teaches austerity, dharma, dependent arising and the path that cuts off becoming
a Buddha-sun will arise to drive off the darkness of wrong and keep living beings safe

manimekalai:21:172-190.reading: Thuvathikan foretells that after many deeds of dharma her life will end in Kanchi, and that in every birth after it in northern Magadha she will be born a man, never leave the dharma of compassion, clear away delusion, and become chief disciple of the great one who gives dharma to others, cutting dependence and so being saved; it adds that the Manimekala goddess, who once lifted her ancestor from the waves, came to her in the grove and bore her to Manipallavam because she had fed the sage Sadhuchakkaran; hearing this, Manimekalai leaves her sea of grief like a peacock freed from a net, and the sun wakes the world.
manimekalai:21:172-190.nuance: Release is placed several births away and in a male body: the epic's prophecy makes rebirth as a man a step before discipleship, which is the epic's view, stated without comment. The closing simile, a peacock freed from the net, answers the unit's opening grief; what frees her is knowing her births, not any change in the facts.
manimekalai:21:172-190.event: Thuvathikan foretells Manimekalai's future births and release and explains why the goddess saved her, and Manimekalai's grief leaves her at dawn.

claims.claim: one who keeps the dharma of compassion through births, born a man, becomes the chief disciple of the Buddha and is freed by cutting dependence

links.note: Brahmadharman foretold that Rahulan would die of the snake's poison glance; the pillar deity now names the deed that set his deaths in motion: the cook he killed in anger at the sage's meal.
links.teaches: The prophecy of kaathai 9 gave only the event; paired with this unit it shows the epic withholding a cause for twelve kaathais and then placing it inside an act of service to the very sage who made the prophecy.

links.note: To the killer Kanchanan the same deity said that karma took the prince's life yet his own cruel deed would not leave him; to Manimekalai it says the prince's death is the fruit of his own killing.
links.teaches: Together the two speeches show the epic's karma as a chain in which every link is also a fresh wrong: the victim's old deed ripens only through a new killing whose doer is held to account in turn.

links.note: The Naladiyar's old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the deity says the cook's killing came 'here' to strike the man reborn as the prince.
links.teaches: The quatrain's deed that seeks out its doer becomes in the epic a deed that crosses a death and a new body, so the 'doer' it finds is a person with another name who does not remember the act.

gains.a: an image for the deed's active search, which the deity states only as a bare claim
gains.b: a case that sets the search across births, which the quatrain does not say

links.note: The couplet says harm done to others comes back on the doer of itself; the deity applies this to a killing done in zeal to serve a holy man and denies that the service exempts it.
links.teaches: The couplet does not ask whether a good motive changes the return of harm; the epic answers that it does not, and names the excuse it rejects, that the master served will protect his servant.

gains.a: a general rule against which the deity's denial of the pious excuse is measured
gains.b: a test of whether intention to serve dharma can stop harm from returning, which the couplet leaves open

links.note: The deity foretells that the materialist will call her knowledge of a former birth a dream sent by a deity; in Vanji he says those deluded by a god or by dreams have changed minds.
links.teaches: The prophecy foretells the opponent's very objection, so when the debate comes the reader already knows the materialist's charge is aimed at a real divine intervention that the epic itself narrated.

links.note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the planted stone called a god and asks whether it will speak while the Lord is within; the pillar deity grants that stone and wood do not speak but says deities the wise install in them stay and speak to men.
links.teaches: Both start from the same premise, that the stone itself is mute; they part over whether a power can be lodged in it, the epic answering yes for guardian deities of a city and the Siddhar answering that the Lord is found only within.

gains.a: a sharp statement of the sceptic's objection that the deity's account is built to meet
gains.b: evidence that the 'speaking stone' it mocks had a worked-out defence, the deity bound to its place, rather than naive idol worship

links.note: Thuvathikan foretells famine in Kanchi and Manimekalai's coming with the bowl; when she arrives, the Kanchi king says all the pillar image's words have come true (கந்திற்பாவை கட்டுரை எல்லாம் வாய் ஆகின்று).
links.teaches: The epic closes its own prophecy by having a king cite the pillar image by name, so the deity's claim at 112 to 129 that installed gods speak true is confirmed inside the story, not only asserted.

links.note: The couplet says that if the sky fails, hunger stays and torments the wide world; the deity foretells the bowl of dharma that gives rain's plenty to a parched world.
links.teaches: Where the couplet treats hunger after drought as beyond remedy, the epic answers it with organized charity, the begging bowl standing in for the failed rain.

gains.a: a statement of the stakes: drought brings hunger even to a world ringed with water
gains.b: a remedy the couplet does not consider, feeding by alms when the sky fails

links.note: Tirumular's grace-power descends as the guru when good and bad deeds are balanced and the soul becomes Siva; the epic's Manimekalai, after births of compassion, becomes a disciple and is saved by cutting dependence herself (சார்பு அறுத்து உய்தி).
links.teaches: Both put a teacher at the threshold of release, but in Tirumular the teacher is grace that ends the soul's own agency, while in the epic the great one only gives dharma and the disciple does the cutting, so they disagree over who acts in release.

gains.a: a sharp contrast that shows how far the epic keeps release in the disciple's own hands
gains.b: a Buddhist counter-model of the teacher-disciple bond without descent of grace

new_concepts.gloss: the cause or condition that must ripen before an event, above all before awakening or release; in the Manimekalai's phrase ஏது நிகழ்ச்சி, the coming to pass of that cause
new_concepts.label_source: the kaathai's own word: ஏது நிகழ்ச்சி (line 160); id as declared in manimekalai ch008 and ch010

new_concepts.gloss: dependence, the chain of conditions that sustains becoming; சார்பின் தோற்றம் is dependent arising, and cutting சார்பு is release
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own words: சார்பின் தோற்றம் (163), சார்பு அறுத்து (179)

source_issues: The chapter's units carry the kaathai number 21 (manimekalai:21:...) while the book's chapter number is 22, because the patikam is chapter 1.
Line 184 was repaired for the old-font ௌ / ெள confusion (தெளிந்தே).

Quotation marks are unbalanced at 106 to 111 (a quote closes after நகுதி and new ones open at 107 and 109) and at 145, where a closing mark after துவதிகன் உரைக்கும் leaves the speaker of 145 to 146 unclear.
Lines 5 to 8 say Manimekalai heard the pillar image's words to Kanchanan (kaathai 20, 110 to 126) though she lay senseless; the text gives no means.
